text:
Over the coming 12 months, more than half of the EU’s electorate will go to the polls in elections that could change the direction of the continent, with attention focused on voters in four of the bloc’s five biggest states.
In Spain, France and Poland, elections could bring the far right into government. Italy’s far-right prime minister looks likely to remain in power, but is under pressure from a challenger even more to the right.
While few of Europe’s far-right parties want to leave the EU, they still see the bloc as a top-down project that undermines national sovereignty and are bent on transforming it into something far looser.
 
The graphics below map the main political parties in each country along two ideological axes – economic left-right and libertarian-authoritarian – using data from researchers at the Chapel Hill Expert Survey. Polling averages then show how the race is developing.
 
Spain
Parliamentary election on 29 November
Spain will head to the polls on Sunday to vote in a sixth general election in 11 years. The snap election could end eight years of socialist-led rule and bring a far-right party into government.
Since the restoration of democracy in Spain in 1977, every prime minister has come from one of three parties: the now-disbanded Union of the Democratic Centre, a very broad centrist alliance from the time of the transition; the centre-right People’s party (PP); and the centre-left Socialist Workers’ party (PSOE).
Often the ruling party has needed the support of smaller parties, sometimes regional groups. But, as elsewhere in Europe, the traditional centre-right and centre-left parties are being challenged by populists further to the left and right.
Since 2023, Pedro Sánchez has been in government with the support of Sumar, which sits ideologically to the left of his PSOE party. But polling suggests that PSOE and Sumar’s latest incarnation, Broad Front, will together fail to muster a majority in parliament.
That leaves the door partly open to the PP, led by Alberto Núñez Feijóo, but he too will need support, and just as Sánchez looked to his left, it is thought Feijóo will look to his right, bringing the far-right Vox of Santiago Abascal into government. Abascal this week told a rally that “remigration sounds to me like heavenly music”.
France
Presidential election on 18 April and 2 May 2027
 
The sitting president, Emmanuel Macron, has served the maximum two terms and will be an onlooker in spring’s election. If, as usual, no candidate wins 50% in the first round of voting, the two leading candidates go into a runoff two weeks later. Polling suggests that Marine Le Pen, the leader of the far-right Rassemblement National (the National Rally) will be one of those two, for the third time.
But unlike on previous occasions, there is no obvious centrist candidate to challenge her in the second round. The president’s heirs apparent – Gabriel Attal of Macron’s Renaissance party and Édouard Philippe of coalition partners Horizons – are splitting the centrist vote. Both were prime ministers under Macron – but then so were five other politicians.
Raphaël Glucksmann, a former Socialist who left to found his own party, is nonetheless the Socialist and centre-left candidate. He is outflanked on the left by Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who seems most likely to face Le Pen in the second round. In the contest between the far left and far right, the polls suggest Le Pen will be the victor.
Poland
Parliamentary election 11 November 2027
For 20 years, the prime ministers of Poland have come from one of two parties, the hard-right Law and Justice (PiS) party, or the Civic Platform – now Civic Coalition (KO) – of Donald Tusk, a centrist and relatively libertarian party which is in government. The two parties’ starkly opposing ideas and practices have led to constitutional crisis, not least because the PiS holds the presidency.
 
Although polling shows support for the PiS faltering, Tusk can take little comfort – much of that support seems to be flowing toward parties even farther to the right; Konfederacja (Confederation), a libertarian nationalist far-right coalition, and their former allies, the Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP). KKP was last assessed by Chapel Hill researchers in 2024 as part of Konfederacja, but the party is significantly further to the authoritarian right. It is also the only party that advocates Poland’s withdrawal from the EU and faces regular criticism for pro-Russian positions on foreign policy.
Even worse for Tusk, two of his three coalition partners – the centre-right Polska 2050 and the conservative agrarian PSL – are at risk of polling below the 5% threshold needed to enter parliament. Their success or failure in clearing that threshold could play a major role in deciding the election.
Italy
Parliamentary election due by 22 December 2027
 
The last of the big four is Italy, where the far right has been in power since 2022. Giorgia Meloni’s Fratelli d’Italia (Brothers of Italy) party has been in a rightwing coalition with Lega (League) and the relatively centrist Forza Italia.
 
Meloni is odds on to remain prime minister after the election, according to the Polymarket betting site. But she is under pressure, perhaps surprisingly, from the right.
Roberto Vannacci, a retired general, has started a far-right party, Futuro Nazionale (National Future), and is polling at least as well as Meloni’s coalition partners. Vannacci’s party is too new to have been assessed by Chapel Hill researchers, but given that his stated reason for leaving Lega was that it was insufficiently rightwing, it is very probably in the upper right quadrant of the chart.
digest_he:
בחודשים הקרובים צפויים למעלה ממחצית מבעלי זכות הבחירה באיחוד האירופי להשתתף במערכות בחירות שיעצבו מחדש את פני היבשת. המוקד המרכזי יהיה בארבע מתוך חמש המדינות הגדולות באיחוד, שבהן מפלגות הימין הקיצוני מאיימות להשיג השפעה ממשלתית משמעותית או לחזק את כוחן הקיים.

בספרד, בחירות בזק עלולות להביא לסיום השלטון הסוציאליסטי ולשילוב מפלגת הימין הקיצוני קולקס בממשלה. בצרפת, מרין לה פן מסתמנת כמועמדת מובילה לסיבוב השני בבחירות לנשיאות, כאשר קולות המרכז מפוצלים. בפולין, המאבק בין מפלגות השלטון המרכזיות מוביל להתחזקות גורמי ימין קיצוני נוספים. באיטליה, ראשת הממשלה ג'ורג'ה מלוני צפויה להישאר בתפקידה אך ניצבת בפני לחץ מימין.

למרות שרוב מפלגות הימין הקיצוני אינן דורשות את יציאת מדינותיהן מהאיחוד, הן שואפות לשנות את מבנהו כדי לצמצם את הריכוזיות ולחזק את ריבונות המדינות החברות, מגמה העשויה לשנות דרמטית את המפה הפוליטית באירופה.
